title: What Is Machine Learning?
html:
Machine learning builds programs that improve at a task from data instead of from hand-written rules. You supply examples; a learning algorithm finds the parameters of a model that generalises to examples it has never seen.

Machine learning (Mitchell, 1997) — a program learns from experience E with respect to a task T and a performance measure P if its performance at T, measured by P, improves with E. Spam filtering: T = label emails, E = emails people marked as spam or not, P = the share of emails labelled correctly.

Rules vs learning

In traditional programming a person writes the rules. In ML the rules — the model's parameters — are fitted from examples of inputs paired with the right answers.

Data + hand-written rules
→
Program
→
Answers
Data + known answers
→
Learning algorithm
→
Model (learned rules)
→
Answers for new data

A tiny example: the algorithm is never told the rule y = 3x + 2; it recovers it from 50 noisy examples.

The supervised setting

y = f(x) + ε learn f̂ ≈ f from pairs (x₁, y₁), …, (xₙ, yₙ)

f is the unknown true relationship and ε is noise no model can predict (measurement error, missing information). Even a perfect f̂ keeps the error caused by ε — the irreducible error. This picture covers supervised learning; unsupervised learning has no y at all (see Types of Learning).

TermMeaningHouse-price example

ParametersLearned from data during trainingThe weights w₁, w₂, b
HyperparametersChosen before training, tuned on validation dataRegularisation strength, tree depth
Training / fittingAdjusting parameters to reduce a loss on training datamodel.fit(X, y)
Inference / predictionApplying the trained model to new inputsmodel.predict(X_new)
GeneralisationPerforming well on unseen data from the same distributionAccurate prices for next month's listings

Key point

These notes cover classic ML on mostly tabular data. Neural networks are covered in Deep Learning, LLMs and prompting in Generative AI, search/logic/planning in Artificial Intelligence, and NumPy/pandas/plotting in Data Science.

When ML is — and isn't — the right tool

Do

Use ML when rules are too many or unknown (spam, fraud, images), the patterns change over time, there is enough representative data, and occasional errors are acceptable.

Avoid

Using ML when a few clear rules work, when there is no data (or no labels) to learn from, when every decision must be exactly explainable and guaranteed, or when a wrong answer is catastrophic and cannot be caught.

The workflow at a glance

Frame the problem
→
Collect & explore data
→
Split train / validation / test
→
Prepare features
→
Train a baseline, then better models
→
Tune & validate
→
Test once
→
Deploy & monitor

Each box has its own topic in these notes. The split comes before any preprocessing is fitted, and the test set is used once at the end — breaking either rule causes data leakage.

What is the difference between a parameter and a hyperparameter?

Parameters are learned from the training data (regression weights, tree split thresholds). Hyperparameters are set before training and control how learning happens (learning rate, max_depth, regularisation strength C); they are chosen by comparing models on validation data or with cross-validation.

What does it mean for a model to generalise?

It performs about as well on new data from the same distribution as on the data it was trained on. We estimate this with held-out data the model never saw during training or tuning. A model that is excellent on training data but poor on held-out data has overfit.

How is ML different from traditional programming?

Traditional programs apply rules a developer wrote. ML programs apply rules (parameters) that an algorithm fitted from examples, so behaviour comes from the data — which is also why data quality, representativeness and leakage matter so much.
